cards.headline: Scored from a script read on a flight
cards.snippet: Daniel Lopatin, who had worked with the Safdie brothers on earlier films, read the script for Marty Supreme on a flight to Los Angeles in 2023. He began shaping the film's themes in his mind, both its poetic essence and the structure of the score. Later, he and director Josh Safdie worked on the music every day for 10 weeks. Lopatin rented a small studio space in Manhattan to score the film.
cards.context: Force of Life is track 22 of the 23-track score.

cards.headline: Safdie's playlist: New Order to Peter Gabriel
cards.snippet: While Daniel Lopatin was composing the score for Marty Supreme, director Josh Safdie put together a Spotify playlist to steer him. It featured artists such as New Order, Tears for Fears, Peter Gabriel, Fats Domino and Constance Demby. The film takes place in the 1950s, and that setting led to what the source calls a "radical use of electronica" in the score.
cards.context: The film is set in the 1950s, yet the score leans on electronic sounds.

cards.headline: Pitchfork's first Best New Music for a film score
cards.snippet: Daniel Lopatin's Marty Supreme score, released December 25, 2025 alongside the film, became the first film score Pitchfork designated Best New Music. In its review, Pitchfork's Sam Goldner pointed to the ending of the film and called Lopatin's "Force of Life" gorgeous. He wrote that the track complicates the film's commentary on ambition, evoking how limitless and meaningless dreams can be.
cards.context: Pitchfork's Sam Goldner called the track gorgeous and said it complicates the film's take on ambition.

cards.headline: The film's whole life cycle in one line
cards.snippet: The movie began with sperm cells creating the Marty Supreme ball. It ended with Marty seeing the product of his sperm cells.
cards.context: Refers to the opening credits, where an egg becomes a ping-pong ball, and the film's ending.

cards.headline: An ode to winning only for yourself
cards.snippet: There is nothing better in the world than winning for yourself.
cards.context: Reacting to the film's final triumph and how this track scores it.

cards.headline: The 1950s called, it wants its synths back
cards.snippet: The soundtrack to Marty Supreme is so good that it makes you forget how out of place 80s synths sound in a story set in the 50s.
cards.context: Critics noted the same deliberate anachronism: a 1952 story with an '80s-flavoured score.

cards.headline: Stranger Things composers vs. Tangerine Dream
cards.snippet: I like Kyle Dixon/Michael Stein, but they rely so much on just synths. This sounds like Tangerine Dream. It's so layered.
cards.context: Compares Lopatin to the Stranger Things composers; a critic also cited Tangerine Dream.

cards.headline: Closes the film Marty Supreme
cards.snippet: Track 22 on Lopatin's 2025 score for Josh Safdie's A24 film, which stars Timothée Chalamet as table tennis hopeful Marty Mauser.
cards.context: Lopatin previously scored the Safdies' Good Time and Uncut Gems.
